title: Ezekiel 26:1–14
context: In the eleventh year, in the first of the month, the LORD’s word comes to Ezekiel. The prophet, addressed as “son of man,” is told that Tyre has said against Jerusalem, “Aha! She is broken! She who was the gateway of the peoples has been returned to me. I will be replenished, now that she is laid waste;” Because of that taunt, the Lord GOD is against Tyre and will cause many nations to come up against her, as the sea causes its waves to come up. Walls and towers will fall; her dust will be scraped away; she will be a bare rock, a place for the spreading of nets in the middle of the sea, and plunder for the nations. Her daughters in the field will be slain with the sword, and they will know that he is the LORD. The Lord GOD then says he will bring on Tyre Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, king of kings, from the north, with horses, chariots, horsemen, and a great army. A siege is described: forts, a mound, a buckler, battering engines, axes, the dust of horses, shaken walls, gates entered as a city broken open, streets trodden, people killed, pillars down, riches plundered, stones and timber and dust laid in the waters. Songs and harps will cease. She will be a bare rock, a place for nets, and will be built no more, for the LORD has spoken it. The oracle is dated to the eleventh year, on the first of the month, without naming the month. 2 Kings 25 and Jeremiah 39 and 52 place Jerusalem’s fall in the eleventh year as well, and those accounts stand beside this heading without being blended into one day. The chapter names Nebuchadnezzar as the king brought against Tyre, with many nations like waves. Ezekiel 29:17–20 will speak again of Nebuchadnezzar and Tyre. That later word is named here without harmonizing the two passages. Later readers often compare a long Babylonian siege and a later taking of the island; this chapter does not narrate those later events, and it does not settle the later history of the site.

verses.text: In the eleventh year, in the first of the month, the LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
“In the eleventh year, in the first of the month, the LORD’s word came to me, saying,” The word is dated to the eleventh year, on the first of the month. The month itself is not named. 2 Kings 25 and Jeremiah 39 and 52 also speak of the eleventh year in connection with Jerusalem’s fall; those narratives and this heading may be read side by side, and they are not turned into a single calendar line in the oracle.

Arminian readers take the date as a real moment in the prophet’s hearing, a word that arrives in the same span of years as the city’s fall, and that now turns to Tyre.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same eleventh year and first of the month as the LORD’s own timing of the word that follows, a dated speech against Tyre.

Shared ground: the oracle is fixed to the eleventh year, on the first of the month. The missing month-name is a fact of the heading, not a gap to be filled from another book.

verses.text: “Son of man, because Tyre has said against Jerusalem, ‘Aha! She is broken! She who was the gateway of the peoples has been returned to me. I will be replenished, now that she is laid waste;’
verses.arminianNotes:
“Son of man, because Tyre has said against Jerusalem, ‘Aha! She is broken! She who was the gateway of the peoples has been returned to me. I will be replenished, now that she is laid waste;’” The prophet is “son of man” again, and the because is Tyre’s own mouth. “Aha!” is the same cry Ammon made, now spoken over a broken Jerusalem, the gateway of the peoples, as if her traffic had come back to Tyre, who expects to be replenished by the waste. The taunt is commercial and glad, and it is told in Tyre’s words.

Arminian readers hear a port-city’s joy over a neighbor’s breaking, a hope of gain from Jerusalem’s ruin, and a word the LORD treats as the reason he is against Tyre.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same “Aha!”, the claim that the gateway of the peoples has been returned, and the hope of being replenished, as Tyre’s own speech, the Lord GOD’s stated ground for what follows.

Shared ground: Tyre’s offense is this taunt over Jerusalem. The gateway and the replenishing are her own account of the gain she sees.

verses.text: therefore the Lord GOD says, ‘Behold, I am against you, Tyre, and will cause many nations to come up against you, as the sea causes its waves to come up.
verses.arminianNotes:
“therefore the Lord GOD says, ‘Behold, I am against you, Tyre, and will cause many nations to come up against you, as the sea causes its waves to come up.” The LORD is against Tyre, and many nations will come up as waves come up from the sea. The image fits a city of the sea: what she lives by will be the likeness of her judgment, wave after wave of nations.

Arminian readers hear a “therefore” that answers the “Aha!”, a coming of many nations, not one only, and a word Tyre can recognize as spoken against her pride in the sea.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same “I am against you, Tyre,” and the many nations coming up as the sea causes its waves to come up, as the Lord GOD’s appointed answer.

Shared ground: many nations will come up like waves. The next verses will also name Nebuchadnezzar, and both names belong to the one word.

verses.text: They will destroy the walls of Tyre, and break down her towers. I will also scrape her dust from her, and make her a bare rock.
verses.arminianNotes:
“They will destroy the walls of Tyre, and break down her towers. I will also scrape her dust from her, and make her a bare rock.” The nations will destroy walls and break towers; the LORD himself will scrape her dust and make her a bare rock. The stripping is complete, down to rock, a city with even its dust taken away.

Arminian readers hear walls and towers down, and a scraping to bare rock, a humiliation of the strong place that had rejoiced when Jerusalem was broken.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the destroyed walls, the broken towers, the scraped dust, and the bare rock as the LORD’s work, done by the nations he brings up and by his own scraping.

Shared ground: Tyre is brought down to bare rock. The image will return at the end of the unit, a place for nets.

verses.text: She will be a place for the spreading of nets in the middle of the sea; for I have spoken it,’ says the Lord GOD. ‘She will become plunder for the nations.
verses.arminianNotes:
“She will be a place for the spreading of nets in the middle of the sea; for I have spoken it,” says the Lord GOD. “She will become plunder for the nations.” The bare rock is in the middle of the sea, useful for spreading nets, and she will be plunder. The LORD has spoken it. A fishing-ground replaces a gateway of the peoples, and the word is bound to his having spoken.

Arminian readers hear a port reduced to a place for nets, plunder for the nations, a reversal of the replenishing Tyre had promised herself, and a word that stands because he has spoken it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the spreading of nets in the middle of the sea, the spoken word of the Lord GOD, and the plunder for the nations as his own settled outcome for Tyre.

Shared ground: she will be a place for nets, and plunder, because he has spoken it. The maritime city is judged in maritime terms.

verses.text: Her daughters who are in the field will be slain with the sword. Then they will know that I am the LORD.’
verses.arminianNotes:
“Her daughters who are in the field will be slain with the sword. Then they will know that I am the LORD.” The daughters in the field fall by the sword, and they will know that he is the LORD. Many readers take the daughters in the field as dependent towns on the mainland; the verse itself says “daughters who are in the field” and the death is told in that one clause, without further description.

Arminian readers hear outlying towns under the sword, a knowledge of the LORD that comes through that fall, a word that still has the familiar close of the book.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the slaying of the daughters in the field with the sword, and the knowledge that he is the LORD, as his own word over those settlements and over Tyre.

Shared ground: the daughters in the field fall by the sword, and they will know that he is the LORD. The line is sober, and it is enough.

verses.text: “For the Lord GOD says: ‘Behold, I will bring on Tyre Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, king of kings, from the north, with horses, with chariots, with horsemen, and an army with many people.
verses.arminianNotes:
“For the Lord GOD says: ‘Behold, I will bring on Tyre Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, king of kings, from the north, with horses, with chariots, with horsemen, and an army with many people.” The waves of nations now have a named king: Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, called king of kings, coming from the north with a full force. 2 Kings 25 and Jeremiah 39 and 52 tell of this same king against Jerusalem in these years; Ezekiel 29:17–20 will speak again of Nebuchadnezzar and Tyre. Those texts stand beside this bringing, and are not merged with it in this verse.

Arminian readers hear a named invader, a king of Babylon brought by the LORD, a force of horses and people, a word Tyre can hear as more than a figure of waves.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the bringing of Nebuchadnezzar, king of kings from the north, with horses, chariots, horsemen, and many people, as the Lord GOD’s own act against Tyre.

Shared ground: Nebuchadnezzar is the king named, and the LORD is the one who brings him. The army is described in the next verses as a siege.

verses.text: He will kill your daughters in the field with the sword. He will make forts against you, cast up a mound against you, and raise up the buckler against you.
verses.arminianNotes:
The king from the north will kill the daughters in the field with the sword, and will raise siege-works: forts, a mound, and a buckler against the city. The assault is a field campaign and a formal siege, told in the language of ramps and shields, not as a scene to be enlarged. The daughters in the field appear again, as in verse 6.

Arminian readers hear a siege that closes in, forts and a mound against the walls, a word that treats Tyre as a city that can be approached and pressed, as Jerusalem was pressed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the killing in the field, the forts, the mound, and the buckler as the work of the king the LORD has brought, the first acts of the siege the following verses will continue.

Shared ground: the field and the walls are both under attack. The siege tools are named, and the description stays that of a campaign.

verses.text: He will set his battering engines against your walls, and with his axes he will break down your towers.
verses.arminianNotes:
Battering engines will be set against the walls, and axes will break down the towers. The siege now has engines and axes, the tools for walls and towers already condemned to fall. The picture is still a military one, and it is given in those two strokes.

Arminian readers hear walls under engines and towers under axes, a breaking down that answers Tyre’s confidence as a strong city of the sea, a word she can still take as warning.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the battering engines against the walls and the axes against the towers as the appointed means of the breaking already named in verse 4.

Shared ground: engines and axes come against walls and towers. The siege language continues, and is not turned into a spectacle.

verses.text: By reason of the abundance of his horses, their dust will cover you. Your walls will shake at the noise of the horsemen, of the wagons, and of the chariots, when he enters into your gates, as men enter into a city which is broken open.
verses.arminianNotes:
The abundance of horses will raise a dust that covers the city, and the walls will shake at the noise of horsemen, wagons, and chariots, when the king enters the gates as men enter a city which is broken open. The entry is the entry of a breached city, noisy and thick with dust. The gates, once a boast, become the way in for the army.

Arminian readers hear a city entered as a broken city, walls shaking at the noise, a fall that is public and unmistakable, the end of the “Aha!” that began the oracle.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the covering dust of the horses, the shaking walls, and the entry into the gates as into a city broken open, as the LORD’s bringing of this king all the way in.

Shared ground: the gates are entered, and the city is broken open. The noise and the dust are the oracle’s own images of that entry.

verses.text: He will tread down all your streets with the hoofs of his horses. He will kill your people with the sword. The pillars of your strength will go down to the ground.
verses.arminianNotes:
The hoofs of the horses will tread down all the streets; the people will be killed with the sword; the pillars of her strength will go down to the ground. Streets, people, and pillars fall together. The killing is named in one clause, and is not described further. The pillars of strength, whatever proud monuments they were, go down to the ground.

Arminian readers hear a city walked over by horses, a people under the sword, and strength’s pillars down, a complete street-level fall that still speaks as the LORD’s word against the taunt.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the trodden streets, the people killed with the sword, and the pillars of strength gone down to the ground as the work of the king brought from the north.

Shared ground: streets, people, and pillars are all down. The sword is named, and the line is left in that restraint.

verses.text: They will make a plunder of your riches and make a prey of your merchandise. They will break down your walls and destroy your pleasant houses. They will lay your stones, your timber, and your dust in the middle of the waters.
verses.arminianNotes:
“They will make a plunder of your riches and make a prey of your merchandise. They will break down your walls and destroy your pleasant houses. They will lay your stones, your timber, and your dust in the middle of the waters.” Riches and merchandise become plunder and prey; walls and pleasant houses are broken; stones, timber, and dust are laid in the middle of the waters. The sea receives what the city was built of. The “they” of this verse sits beside the single king of the earlier lines, as the many nations and the one army already named.

Arminian readers hear a trading city’s wealth taken, its pleasant houses destroyed, and its very building stuff thrown into the waters, a reversal of the replenishing Tyre had expected from Jerusalem’s waste.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the plunder of riches and merchandise, the broken walls and destroyed houses, and the stones, timber, and dust laid in the waters, as the outcome the LORD has spoken against Tyre.

Shared ground: the wealth goes as plunder, and the fabric of the city goes into the waters. The sea is the grave of the stones.

verses.text: I will cause the noise of your songs to cease. The sound of your harps won’t be heard any more.
verses.arminianNotes:
“I will cause the noise of your songs to cease. The sound of your harps won’t be heard any more.” Songs and harps go quiet. The LORD himself causes the noise of the songs to cease. A city famous for its trade and, in this line, for its music, is left without that sound.

Arminian readers hear a silence where there had been songs, a ceasing the LORD causes, a loss of joy in the same mouth that had said “Aha!” over Jerusalem.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the ceasing of the songs and the unheard harps as the LORD’s own act, the end of Tyre’s sound.

Shared ground: the music stops, and it will not be heard any more. The judgment has reached even the city’s songs.

verses.text: I will make you a bare rock. You will be a place for the spreading of nets. You will be built no more; for I the LORD have spoken it,’ says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes:
“I will make you a bare rock. You will be a place for the spreading of nets. You will be built no more; for I the LORD have spoken it,” says the Lord GOD. The bare rock and the nets return, and a further word is added: “You will be built no more”. The LORD has spoken it. How that word stands beside later settlement on the site is a question the chapter itself does not take up. The unit ends on the spoken word, as verse 5 also did.

Arminian readers hear a city left as a rock for nets, and a “built no more” that belongs to the LORD’s spoken resolve, a close that does not invite a later history to be written into the verse.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the bare rock, the place for nets, the “built no more” and the “I the LORD have spoken it” as the Lord GOD’s own close to this first movement against Tyre.

Shared ground: she will be a bare rock and a place for nets, and the LORD has spoken it. The later history of the site is not narrated in this verse.
